title: Everything you need to know about the Madring
excerpt:
The 2026 season continues this weekend with the Spanish Grand Prix, with the Madring making its debut. But how much do you know about the new circuit? F1.com presents your all-in-one guide…

Key Madring statistics

Circuit length: 5.414km

Number of turns: 22

Number of laps: 57

Race distance: 308.399km

Lap record: N/A

When was Madrid's first Grand Prix?

This weekend marks the first time F1 has raced at the Madring, but the Spanish capital is no stranger to the sport, having first held the Spanish Grand Prix in 1968 at Jarama.

Located 30km north of the city – significantly further out than the new venue – Jarama was added to the calendar in rotation with Barcelona's Montjuic Circuit as part of a concerted effort by the country to establish itself on the international racing stage.

A tragic accident at Montjuic resulted in Madrid becoming the permanent host between 1976 and 1979, and once more in 1981, with winners including James Hunt and Mario Andretti.

The event didn't take place for a number of years due to a lack of interest and unpleasant weather conditions and, by the time it returned, Jerez and Barcelona were selected as preferable locations.

What's the circuit like to drive?

The short answer is that none of the drivers will know for sure until Free Practice 1 gets underway on Friday, September 11, although the layout and useful test that Formula 3 completed give us some indication.

First up is the short run of about 200m down to Turn 1, before a right-hander launches the drivers around the third corner, leading onto the longest straight on the circuit. The speed picks up massively until they arrive at a heavy braking zone, followed by an elevation change and blind apex at Turn 8.

The street section comes to an end and switches to the permanent track, where a chicane paves the way for La Monumental – an ambitious and exhilarating banked curve with a 24% gradient. Thousands of fans will roar drivers around here, with multiple racing lines on offer to encourage a myriad of moves.

Another flat-out series of turns comes next, but then precision will be critical as the walls begin to close in and the track enters a twisty and technical section, culminating in the final tight corner back onto the start/finish straight.

Where are the Straight Mode zones and overtake detection?

As a reminder, and as explained in our pre-season summary of regulation changes, Straight Mode is a different aerodynamic configuration that allows cars to reduce their drag, making them more efficient when accelerating up towards top speed.

The rear wing continues to open up a gap – just like it did when drivers used DRS (the Drag Reduction System) in the past – but now the front wing also moves. The uppermost front wing elements drop down at the same time the rear wing’s top element does.

This is a mode that is used on every single lap in dry conditions, in every area that is designated for it. Essentially, the car will adapt between two different configurations depending on where it is on the track, providing maximum downforce in corners but then less drag on straights.

At the Madring, there are just two designated Straight Mode zones: a run along the start/finish straight, followed by the section between Turns 3 and 4.

Meanwhile, Overtake Mode replaces DRS and is a new power mode that allows a driver to recharge more electrical energy, and generate an additional electrical power profile, so they can sustain a higher speed for a longer period.

There is one detection point per lap for this mode – expected to be out of the final corner on many occasions, leading onto a long straight – and it will be available to drivers on the following lap as long as they stay within a second of the car in front at that detection point.

The Overtake Detection marker here comes just before the entry to Turn 22, while the Overtake Activation line follows on the exit of that corner, heading onto the start/finish straight.

Five fun facts about the Spanish Grand Prix

The circuit combines public roads with purpose-built sections around IFEMA Madrid and Valdebebas, making it a hybrid venue

Madrid-born Carlos Sainz will experience his first true home race, with the Spaniard taking on the role of circuit ambassador

The cars are expected to reach a top speed of 340kph

Around 45,000 spectators will watch drivers at La Monumental, which is 550m long and features banking with a gradient of up to 24%

The Madring is the first track to debut on the F1 calendar since Las Vegas was added in 2023

title: Facts, stats and trivia ahead of the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix
excerpt:
Round 14 of the 2026 season gets underway this weekend at the brand-new Madring, which is set to host the Spanish Grand Prix as Formula 1 returns to the nation's capital for the first time in over 40 years.

Free Practice 1 and 2 will take place on Friday, September 11, followed by Free Practice 3 and Qualifying on Saturday, September 12, and the Grand Prix itself on Sunday, September 13.

Vital statistics

First Grand Prix – 2026

Track Length – 5.414km

Lap record – N/A

Most pole positions – N/A

Most wins – N/A

Trivia – This won't be the first time that Madrid has welcomed F1 as the Circuito del Jarama, north of the capital, held nine rounds of the World Championship between 1968 and 1981

Pole run to Turn 1 braking point – 200 metres

Overtakes completed in 2025 – N/A

Safety Car probability – N/A

Virtual Safety Car probability – N/A

Pit stop time loss – N/A

Tyre and strategy insight

"The start-finish line and Turn 1 are separated by just 200 metres," reads Pirelli's weekend preview, with the compounds available this weekend being the C2 (as the hard), C3 (as the medium) and C4 (as the soft).

"The first sector is very fast and leads into a second section featuring several medium and low-speed corners, including the banked Turn 12. The final part of the lap also includes a number of 90-degree corners similar to those drivers encounter in Baku.

"Pirelli's work to identify the forces that tyres will be subjected to at the Madring began three years ago, when the designers provided the first information on the final layout. Using simulation tools, the trajectories that the cars would follow around the circuit were identified and, consequently, the loads to which the tyres would be exposed were calculated.

"Once the circuit had been completed, a group of Pirelli engineers visited the venue to measure the asphalt's macro and micro roughness, refine the simulations and produce a technical briefing document that was shared with the teams to support their preparation for this new event.

What time is the 2026 Spanish GP and how can I watch it?

"From an energy perspective, the Madrid circuit ranks among the five most demanding on the calendar, with lateral forces comparable in intensity to those recorded at Barcelona and Silverstone. The "Monumental" is the corner that generates the highest vertical load of the season, not only because of its banking but also because of its length.

"Its configuration will also present a significant challenge in terms of tyre grip. Drivers may adopt different approaches when tackling it, depending on how much they wish to prioritise the opportunity to attack into the following corner.

"The asphalt is very smooth and therefore offers a relatively low level of grip. For this reason, it has been treated with high-pressure water jets, as is already done at other circuits, including Singapore, to remove dust and oily residues typically associated with newly laid surfaces."

Current form

Kimi Antonelli increased his lead in the drivers' standings with a superb recovery drive from P19 to win his home race at Monza, giving him a 66-point advantage over his Mercedes team mate George Russell, with Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton a further 10 points adrift.

An incredible back-and-forth battle between the Silver Arrows pair unfolded during the Italian Grand Prix, but it was Antonelli who came out on top to match Russell's career tally of seven victories.

They still both face plenty of serious competition from outside the team, especially from Ferrari, with the squad suffering an agonising event on home soil that saw Hamilton and Charles Leclerc clash on the opening lap before the latter crashed out in a separate incident.

While Hamilton has called on Ferrari to "change things" when it comes to the intra-team battle, Fred Vasseur would only hint at a discussion around implementing team orders – a topic which similarly came up at McLaren.

Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri were allowed to race freely over the closing stages and the reigning World Champion ultimately succeeded in securing P4, with the weekend marking a slight downturn in performance after he clinched victories in Hungary and the Netherlands.

Elsewhere, Max Verstappen enjoyed his fifth podium of the season with a low-key drive while Liam Lawson – continuing to step in for the injured Isack Hadjar – failed to fight back into points contention following a grid penalty.

His regular team faced another twist in the midfield contest as their closest rivals snatched an unexpected pole position with Pierre Gasly. He wasn't able to maintain the pace on race day and dropped back to P7, leading Arvid Lindblad, the second Alpine of Franco Colapinto, and Lawson's substitute Yuki Tsunoda.

title: De la Rosa on how Aston Martin’s risky upgrades paid off
excerpt:
Pedro de la Rosa has delved into “one of the best moments we've had so far” when Fernando Alonso shared his approval of Aston Martin's upgrade package in Hungary, with the squad's Team Representative admitting that he was “very nervous” about their unique schedule.

The beginning of the season came with plenty of challenges for the Silverstone-based outfit as they struggled with reliability issues and a lack of performance, leading them to focus their efforts on delivering a B-spec of the 2026 car in Round 11.

It seemed like a bold approach, especially at a time when their rivals were spreading upgrades over multiple race weekends, but it paid off – the heavily revised AMR26 got ahead of Cadillac and Williams in Qualifying before further progress came in the form of a new Honda power unit in the Netherlands.

On the latest episode of the official F1 podcast Beyond The Grid, De la Rosa provided some insight into just how much relied on the success of the upgrades.

‘Everything worked as planned’

De la Rosa conceded that he wasn’t certain just how much performance the changes would bring, but it didn’t take long for Alonso to give his verdict.

“I would lie if I said I was not very nervous because you are expecting, you are hoping, you've been waiting a long time, and then the car just starts,” he said. “I looked at the car and the side pods were so small, the radiators look the smallest I've ever seen in my life.

“And I thought ‘OK, the aero numbers are promising, but maybe the cooling is not enough.’ Or you start thinking about many other scenarios where I've been, because I've been in most of the most unwanted scenarios in F1. But everything worked as planned.

“Then after the installation lap, you looked around and the people were relieved because everything was working as expected. With Fernando, I know him so much that we look at the eyes. I always try to be at the front of the car when he comes in after a run. He looks at me, I look at him, and I know exactly what he's thinking.

“I don't even need to listen to the radio. And his eyes look like, ‘yes, it's working.’ Sometimes we've had upgrades in the past and I look at him and he immediately doesn't want to look at my eyes. When he tries to refuse the eye contact, I know we are in trouble. But that time he looked and he was just like, ‘yeah, it's there, it's there.’

Alonso details why he's in no hurry to make call on his future

“It was a very exciting moment. You always have to focus on things you can change, you can do, you can improve. That was, OK, not where we wanted to be, I repeat again, but it was one of the best moments we've had so far this season.”

With ongoing speculation around Alonso’s future in the sport, his reaction was the boost the team needed, although De la Rosa stated that the upgrades were never going to sway the Spaniard.

Asked whether the strategy risked losing their star driver, he replied: “I think that decision was never based [on] if we lost anyone or anything. I think that Fernando, whatever his decision will be, you have to believe in a project, you know, not if the car is quick on the next race.

“I think Fernando is so wise, he's learned so much, that it's either you believe in the project or you don't. It's not whether we managed to improve the car for the summer break as we were expecting.”

Being ‘in good hands’ with Adrian Newey

One of the factors that made Aston Martin’s initial difficulties such a shock to fans was last season’s addition of Adrian Newey, who is widely regarded as one of the most successful car designers in the sport’s history.

With years of experience at teams like Williams and Red Bull, many believed that the Briton would quickly transform Aston Martin and take them closer to the front in his latest role as Team Principal.

While it hasn’t gone that way quite yet, De la Rosa was satisfied with how easily Newey has settled into the outfit and offered a new interpretation of the traditional team boss responsibilities.

How an unraced Newey-designed McLaren compares to Aston Martin’s 2026 car

“I must say that Team Principal is a title,” he explained. “It's not a job description. Adrian has said it many times. We are fortunate in the team having Mike Krack as well, an experienced Team Principal, now chief track operations.

“But when Adrian is not at the racetrack, Mike acts like a Team Principal. I think we have a very luxurious situation where we have people working in different areas covering for when Adrian is not here. Other teams have different structures.

“It's quite ambiguous now what a Team Principal job description really is. In my time, you had a Team Principal that was taking all the decisions. But now you have a Team Principal and normally you also have a CEO on top of them. I think that we have a very good structure. As long as Adrian feels comfortable and competitive, we're in good hands.”

Taking steps towards where they want to be

Aston Martin have made it clear that scrapping for points – which they’ve achieved on two occasions in 2026 with Alonso – is far from their ultimate goal, but they’ve got some catching up to do in relation to the frontrunners.

Despite De la Rosa’s admission that F1 is “a business where you arrive always too late”, he was enthused by the progress they’d made, and determined to make even more.

“I think that we are in the upward trend,” he concluded. “I've said it in Australia this year, when we started this, we were nowhere. But all we need to do is improve and never stop improving.

“Obviously, our strategy was different. We didn't improve until the summer, but we've made a big step. We are now in a position we cannot stop. It's just a race of time. The people have done a better job than us. That's why they're winning. We just have to slowly chip away all this difference. That’s where we are.

“Everyone has to feel accountable for the results. Everyone has to feel super motivated. We have an amazing partner in Honda that we've managed to survive very difficult times together. We can’t stop and we won't stop.

“We can do it. It's just a matter of never stop the development path that we are in right now. The only teams that do win are the ones that make the right investments. I believe I'm in the right team that is definitely making the right investments.”

title: 5 storylines we're excited about ahead of the Spanish GP
excerpt:
How time flies, as we reach the end of the European season with a second visit to Spain and a brand new venue in Madrid. Off the back of Kimi Antonelli’s remarkable victory in Monza, it’s time for the drivers and teams to reset for a different challenge as we head to the Madring.

A new track!

Who doesn’t love a new circuit to see the drivers put through their paces? From the iconic venue of Monza – the track that has hosted more Formula 1 World Championship races than any other – we head to the newest circuit on the calendar and the 5.414-kilometre Madring.

Located at the IFEMA Exhibition Centre to the north east of the centre of Madrid, the Madring is part-street circuit, part-permanent venue and will provide a very different test compared to last week’s race. There are tight and twisting complexes, flowing sections and even the heavily banked La Monumental corner that will see fans flanking both sides of the circuit as the cars turn through more than 180 degrees.

Given the proximity of the walls in so many parts of the track, mistakes will certainly be severely punished, but the drivers will need to get up to speed quickly. And they’ll do so at a track that will put a premium on slow-speed corner performance and traction, as well as how well a car can ride bumps and kerbs.

It’s going to be a steep learning curve from the moment the teams hit the track on Friday for Free Practice 1.

Advantage Antonelli in the title race

It’s true that Kimi Antonelli was in an extremely strong position in the Drivers’ Championship even before the Italian Grand Prix, but his remarkable win on Sunday has only increased his hopes of winning his first title.

Antonelli was expected to be in damage limitation mode starting 19th, with George Russell, Lewis Hamilton and Lando Norris all hoping to take points off the championship leader. But with the Italian winning his home race on the same weekend he took a power unit penalty, Antonelli now has a 66-point advantage over Russell, that extends to 76 over Hamilton and 96 over Norris.

Why Antonelli’s Monza win feels like the defining moment of 2026

As impressive as Antonelli’s drive was at Monza, we’ve seen multiple occasions this season where reliability or circumstance has led to big swings in terms of points, and there are still 10 rounds remaining as we arrive in the Spanish capital.

For Russell, the form has been more consistent since the summer break, but he needs to find that little bit more performance to put pressure on Antonelli and take regular points off his team mate. There’s still plenty of time left in the season, but the chasing pack will want to hit back quickly.

Can McLaren return to winning ways?

Given recent form, it is perhaps Norris who is likely to offer the biggest threat over the coming races, with the McLaren most competitive on the recent higher-downforce circuits of the Hungaroring and Zandvoort. Norris won on both occasions, and could be in with a chance of doing so again in Madrid.

The layout should suit McLaren more than Monza did, and despite dampening expectations before the Italian Grand Prix, both cars were in the mix for a podium until the closing stages.

That was also thanks to a strong performance from Oscar Piastri, who has yet to win this season but outqualified Norris for the first time since Monaco, and was fighting with his team mate right up to the flag.

While Mercedes appeared to be in a league of their own for spells of the race in Monza, McLaren know Madrid is the type of venue that they should be more competitive relative to the Constructors’ Championship leaders, and will look to hit back this weekend.

Another chance for Lawson and Tsunoda

After an impressive first half of the season at Red Bull, it has been a frustrating few weeks for Isack Hadjar as he has been unable to race since the summer break due to an injured wrist.

The Frenchman missed the Dutch Grand Prix soon after sustaining the injury in training, and then Red Bull opted to not rush him back for Monza as his recovery continues. While the team say his progress has been positive, they made an even earlier call this week to continue with an unchanged line-up, rather than unnecessarily take a risk with Hadjar returning on a street circuit at this stage.

That means another opportunity for Liam Lawson alongside Max Verstappen, after a frustrating weekend in Monza. Lawson took a power unit penalty so always faced a tough afternoon trying to climb through the field, but picked up damage and needed an extra pit stop that prevented him from scoring points.

Lawson did score at Zandvoort, however, and will look to repeat that result in Madrid, while Yuki Tsunoda has also been in the points since returning to VCARB. The Red Bull reserve was just one place outside the top 10 in Zandvoort, and then went one better with 10th place at Monza to secure double points for the team.

The F3 championship showdown

The European season might be coming to an end for Formula 1 this weekend, but it’s the entire 2026 championship that is concluding in Formula 3. And what a final round it promises to be.

The Madring was always scheduled to host the finale, but the postponement of the Bahrain Grand Prix earlier this year has led to a bumper weekend as an extra Qualifying session and Feature Race will take place in Spain.

The Qualifying sessions run back-to-back on Friday, with a Sprint Race on Saturday morning and then the first Feature in the evening after F1 Qualifying. Then Sunday morning will see the final round that could well prove to be a title decider.

GALLERY: F3 drivers test the 'incredible' Madring circuit

Audi-backed junior Freddie Slater arrives with a 15-point advantage over American Ugo Ugochukwu, with the pair having been locked in a close championship battle all year.

Slater looked set to open up a big lead in Monza as he started the Feature Race from pole position and Ugochukwu languished at the back following a grid penalty and early contact, but a dramatic turn of events saw Slater retire and Ugochukwu recover to finish eighth.

There is a maximum of 67 points available over the weekend - 25 for a Feature Race win, 10 for a Sprint, plus a fastest lap point in every race and two points for pole position for each Feature Race - plus Ernesto Rivera and Theophile Nael are both mathematically still in contention but both need a hugely improbable combination of results.

That means it’s likely to be a fight between rookie Slater and second-year Ugochukwu to follow in the footsteps of Rafael Camara and join the likes of Piastri and Gabriel Bortoleto as an F3 champion.

title: Sainz on bringing F1 back to his home city of Madrid
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz knows what it's like to have a home Grand Prix, the Spaniard having competed in 12 of them in Formula 1 in Barcelona. He knows how to deliver for his home fans, too, having scored in each of the first 10 of those appearances. But never has he raced in a Formula 1 Grand Prix in his home city of Madrid – until now.

This weekend, he'll compete in the Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid, on a new part-street, part-purpose-built 22-turn circuit called the Madring. The 32-year-old has played a key role in the project from acting as an adviser to helping promote it. The passion he has for the event is infectious.

"I've been lucky enough to have a home race pretty much all through my career thanks to the Grand Prix in Barcelona," says Sainz when we chat all things Madrid in the Williams hospitality unit. "The fact that it's a lot closer to my [family] home, only 15 minutes by car, and all my family and all my friends are from there, it's probably going to feel even more special.

title: Carlos Sainz reminds Hamilton-Leclerc of 'responsibility' after Ferrari Monza spat
excerpt:
Former Ferrari driver Carlos Sainz has reminded current Scuderia racers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc of the "responsibility" of representing the team at Monza.

During last week's Italian GP, Hamilton attempted to move up the inside of Leclerc at Turn 1 on the opening lap, but was forced wide and down the order by the Monegasque.

Post-race, Hamilton signalled that the team had no "rules of engagement" whilst indicating that there was no "we" involved, as he felt he was ahead at the Turn 2 apex, whilst Leclerc hit back at the idea of media creating "narratives" around the situation at the team, with Hamilton also indicating that, as the best-placed driver in the championship, he should receive preferential treatment to mount the challenge.

Sainz was Leclerc's team-mate between 2021 and 2024, until he was replaced by Hamilton, with the Spanish driver involved in a wheel-to-wheel battle with Leclerc at the 2023 Italian GP for a podium place - eventually outdueling his team-mate to take third.

Observing the situation, the four-time race winner felt that at Monza, Ferrari drivers should shoulder greater "responsibility" when battling the sister car.

"Well, I don't think it's like some people say that it's none of my business," Sainz told media, including RacingNews365.

"But I can tell you that when you have two competitive teammates, these kinds of situations are always going to happen. Charles and I, always twice, two or three times a year, we always had a bit of a discussion or an argument, but after the race or the morning after, we would call each other and sort it out.

"So, I think it's normal when you're fighting for podiums or wins in a competitive team, and there are situations in Turn 1 or situations in the race or with strategy. You always end up one day not being happy with the way it's being handled, and the next day maybe you've been favoured.

"It's always the same case, and I don't know the way it's being handled right now. But when I was there in Ferrari with Charles, we would always sort it out among ourselves, and we would get on with it.

"I remember in 2023 being quite an intense battle with Charles [at Monza], I don't think we got to the point where we had any arguments that day. We both felt like we kept it as fair as we could for what was at stake.

"We had worse ones than that for sure. But at Monza, you feel an extra level of responsibility of making sure you don't touch the other guy in the other red car because it's Monza.

"I think in general that's the number one rule of motorsport or Formula 1, but maybe Ferrari at Monza means a bit more, and you have that in the back of your head for sure going into every battle."

The article continues below.

Hamilton-Leclerc Ferrari Monza spat

Hamilton, when debriefing media after the sixth-placed finish at Monza, recounted the 'rules of engagement' at Mercedes when Nico Rosberg was his team-mate, and their infamous collisions through 2014-2016.

After Rosberg retired at the end of 2016, he was replaced by Valtteri Bottas, who was asked about those rules of engagement with the Briton.

"That's confidential, contractual stuff," he began.

"So, I mean, every team obviously operates differently. You have different rules, but around that time it was very clear that you need to race fair and clean.

"There are certain rules in certain situations, which I don't want to go into detail. You can use your imagination, but it's just how the sport works.

"And sometimes you get it better. Sometimes you get it worse."

title: Fernando Alonso confirms alternative option to F1 for 2027
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has confirmed that a switch to the World Endurance Championship next year is an option on the table as he weighs up a decision over his future.

Alonso has not yet declared what his intentions for 2027 are, as he has yet to formally commit himself to an F1 extension.

Aston Martin has endured a challenging campaign thus far, with Alonso scoring just three points after 13 rounds.

However, the Silverstone-based squad has voiced its desire to continue with Alonso next season as it targets a jump in the pecking order with its engine partner Honda.

Outside of F1, Aston Martin is set up in the World Endurance Championship - a competition Alonso is well familiar with, having won the 2018-19 title with Toyota, as well as two Le Mans victories.

When asked if a move to WEC is an option for 2027, Alonso told media including RacingNews365: “Yes.”

Alonso has insisted on multiple occasions that his future in F1 will not be measured by the competitiveness of the car, but rather how much he enjoys driving the new regulations.

RacingNews365 understands that no announcement regarding Alonso's future is expected this weekend in Madrid, despite it being a home round for the two-time champion.

Alonso backed this up ahead of the Madrid weekend, insisting any declaration on his future would be “not soon”.

As he focuses on the on-track action, Alonso is expecting a challenging event as the drivers get up to speed around a new street track, which has been tipped by some to cause disruption.

“The track seems difficult, first of all, to learn,” he said.

“Very technical, a lot of kerb-riding, and a couple of high-speed sections where you need to get very close to the walls, which is very attractive and very high adrenaline for a driver.

“Close to Jeddah, some sections. But one thing is the simulator, and then reality always gives you a different feeling.

“So I'm looking forward to FP1 and learning the track from the car and and discover all these details.”

title: Madrid tipped to host chaotic F1 weekend: 'Put my money on a red flag'
excerpt:
Pierre Gasly has stated he would “put my money” on a red flag to make an appearance at the Spanish Grand Prix this weekend.

The event has moved to Madrid, with the Madring Circuit hosting an F1 race event for the first time.

The track is set to pose a significant challenge for the drivers due to its narrow layout and the high-speed corners scattered throughout.

At a recent Formula 3 test at the venue, 19 red flags were deployed across two days - 11 of which were due to collisions with the walls.

Gasly, who enters the weekend having secured pole position last time out at the Italian Grand Prix, is not escaping the drivers to escape unscathed.

“I'll put my money on the red flag, that's for sure,” Gasly told media including RacingNews365.

“Driving-wise in the sim it was very enjoyable and very exciting. I got a good read and feel of pretty much every single wall at every single corner, so actually I know what to do and what not to do.

“But it's going to be very challenging, especially in terms of evolution. Probably a lot of track evolution, slightly awkward braking zones, which are not fully straight - snaky, very twisty-type corners.

“Many corners, a lot of blind [corners], banking, up-and-down, undulation all the way.

“So I expect a very tricky track, challenging for us, which makes it good because you can always aim to do a bit more difference driving-wise.”

Gasly likened the challenge of the track to Monaco, where a very minor mistake can quickly end a driver's session.

“But again, it's a type of track like Monaco, where I think if you make a slight mistake, [it is a] big consequence straight away,” he said.

“It's exciting. At the same time, I think it's going to be quite a disruptive weekend from how easy it will be to have a crash.”

title: Sergio Perez spies Cadillac breakthrough at 'scary' Madring
excerpt:
Sergio Perez believes the "scary" Madring offers Cadillac an opportunity to make a breakthrough and score its first points in F1.

After 13 rounds, the team remains on zero points and in 11th in the constructors', with its best finish being 13th for Valtteri Bottas in China, with Perez's own best being 15th in Monaco.

However, during the race in the Principality, Perez initially crossed the line in 11th on the road, and was then promoted to 10th after Nico Hulkenberg was awarded a penalty.

The Mexican was then himself handed a 10-second penalty for being out of position at the red flag restart, dropping him down to 15th, and crucially, promoting Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso into 10th.

The team has not been in a position to fight for points since, as reliability issues have set in, but given the chaotic nature expected of the new Madring in the Spanish capital, where a recent F3 test featured 19 red flags over two days, Perez feels there is an opportunity for Cadillac to finally get on the board this coming weekend.

"The track itself, it's a proper race track, from what I've seen," Perez told media, including RacingNews365.

"I haven't been on the circuit yet, but from what I've seen on the simulator, it's a proper track. It's a bit scary, I'll say. It reminds me a bit of Jeddah, a good, proper track.

"I don't think there is a place more dangerous than Jeddah; it is already quite dangerous. So I don't think Madrid will be something like on that level. I think nobody knows. We have to wait and see.

"It all depends on what grip level we get, but I think there is no room for error. I think I like those places, as you get punished, and it's very rare. Depending on which corner you make a mistake at, you might get away with it. But in most places, there is no margin for it.

"I definitely think this weekend is an opportunity for us. If we execute a good race, if we are 100% on everything, this could be an opportunity for us."

title: The biggest dangers around the 'car killer' Madring F1 circuit
excerpt:
F1 visits a brand-new race track this weekend, with the Spanish Grand Prix moving to Madrid and the Circuito de Madring.

The high-speed track had its first official test last month when Formula 3 held a two-day event - and at it, there were 11 red flags for incidents involving a hit against the barrier.

A handful of drivers have noted the challenge that they are likely to endure to stay out of the barrier, while Williams team boss James Vowles labelled the track a “car killer”.

With the race weekend just around the corner, which sections of the track are likely to cause issues?

If there’s one spot on the Madring that has caused the most crashes, it’s the chicane at Turns 5 and 6. After a run of over 800 meters, during which the F1 cars reach speeds of up to 340 km/h, drivers must brake hard to slow down to about 80 km/h.

The combination of this hard braking, a tight chicane, and minimal run-off areas makes this the ideal spot for mistakes. During the F3 test, a high number of incidents occurred here.

Immediately after this chicane comes Turn 7, the highest point of the circuit at an elevation of about 697 meters. It is a blind turn over a ridge with a wall that is alarmingly close to the exit.

With the already minimal margin for error and the fact that drivers cannot see the apex while braking, promises plenty of incidents in which drivers hit the wall instead of the apex.

Later in the lap comes Turn 17, a sharp 90-degree turn that leads into a tunnel under the M-11 highway. Concrete walls run close to the track both before and after the turn, while limited visibility makes this section particularly treacherous.

Furthermore, drivers approach this section coming off Turns 14 and 15, where aerodynamic load is already high and turbulent air can reduce the car’s stability. Several crashes during the F3 test underscored the danger of this section.

The iconic Turn 12, “La Monumental”, with its 550-meter length and 24 per cent banking, is the circuit’s signature feature. During the F3 test, virtually nothing happened in the turn.

Nevertheless, it remains a potentially dangerous spot: cars pass through here at around 300 km/h and are subjected to enormous lateral forces for about five seconds. The danger of La Monumental, therefore, lies not so much in the likelihood of a crash, but rather in the severe consequences should a crash occur.

title: Aston Martin warn against 'arrogant' expectations at Madrid F1 debut
excerpt:
Aston Martin chief trackside officer Mike Krack has stated it would be “arrogant” to enter the Madrid F1 weekend seeking to capitalise on the unknowns of a new track.

The Madring, the new host of the Spanish Grand Prix, will make its debut this weekend after several years in the making.

It marks the second home event for Fernando Alonso, who has endured a difficult year with Aston Martin so far, scoring just three championship points.

With all teams starting from scratch at Madrid and no historical data to rely on, it opens the window for an unsettled grid order.

But Krack has played down the expectation that it can lift itself up the order at the event.

“We need to keep our feet on the ground,” Krack told media including RacingNews365.

“We are where we are. We have a new track that we need to identify. We need to see.

“We have done our preparation, but let's not forget we were out of Q1 only once. We have one Q2 this year.

“So speaking about Q3, I think it would be a little bit arrogant, even.”

The Madring has been noted for its challenging layout, with some comparing it to the likes of Jeddah for its high-speed sections.

Following a Formula 3 test that saw 11 red flags for contact with the barrier, it has raised suspicions that there could be multiple incidents throughout the F1 weekend.

Should that be the case, Krack insisted it is important the team is there to pick up the pieces.

“This is on a normal qualifying - what you are saying is, if there is chaos and this kind of thing, you need to be prepared,” he said.

“We try to be prepared as much as we can, but the weekend, when your whole knowledge base is simulation and going around and having a look, you need to start conservatively and build your knowledge step by step.

“You need to try and do this better than the competition, but the competitors are very strong as well.

“At the end of the day, I do not expect a major surprise. But if things turn chaotic, you need to be there and try to grab what you can. And the same applies for Sunday.”

title: Carlos Sainz reveals unanimous 'shocked' response to F1's new Spanish home
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz has revealed that "everyone seemed quite shocked" by the Madring layout following its reveal, with it set to host the Spanish Grand Prix this weekend.

Formula 1 heads to the Spanish capital for the first time at a brand-new street circuit close to Madrid's airport, around the IFEMA exhibition centre.

It is expected to be a wild and chaotic event based on the variety of corner types, including a remarkable banked corner measuring 550m in length named La Monumental.

For Sainz, who was born in Madrid, it is a significant event that he has worked closely with, and he has praised the uniqueness of the layout, which gives it "character".

Next to no F1 running has taken place at the new circuit, the sole exception being a Ferrari filming day earlier this year.

There was, however, a full Formula 3 test at the venue recently, which saw several cars damaged. However, many praised it as an incredible layout.

Madrid is very much expected to be a weekend where the unexpected can happen, with the difficult circuit set to test the drivers, something Sainz is excited about.

Discussing Madrid being a big weekend, Sainz told select media, including RacingNews365: "Yeah, I think we can expect a pretty difficult track.

"I think we've all done it in the DIL in the simulator, and we've seen the F3 test. And yeah, talking to the drivers at the parade, everyone seemed quite shocked by the track that Madrid has come up with, which, I think, in a good way, gives character and something to look forward to.

"It's not a normal track, you know, that just gets added to a calendar; it's something a bit different, with a bit of character.

"We will just need to see if it's a bit too much, or once we get some laps going and start giving some feedback to the FIA and the grand prix."

title: Toto Wolff issues Mercedes warning after Monza high
excerpt:
Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff has insisted the squad should not expect to be as competitive in Madrid this weekend following its success in Monza.

The Brackley-based outfit scored a one-two finish, with Kimi Antonelli rising from 19th on the grid to take his seventh career win.

The result marked Mercedes' first event at which it achieved maximum points since the Chinese Grand Prix, where Antonelli won his maiden race in March .

However, Wolff is expecting the situation to change this weekend at Madrid as F1 arrives at a new circuit, suggesting he expects rival teams to be back in the mix this time around.

“This weekend presents a completely different challenge,” Wolff said.

“The circuit characteristics are much closer to somewhere like Budapest or Zandvoort. We are therefore expecting a very close-fought weekend.

“Our task is to understand the demands of the track in Madrid as quickly as possible and maximise our performance from the first session onwards.

“New circuits create opportunities and unknowns in equal measure.”

Madrid is the latest street track to join the schedule, with additions in recent years including Miami, Las Vegas and Jeddah.

Wolff hailed its inclusion on the calendar, stating it is a shining example of how the sport has grown in recent years.

“Madrid is a global destination city and racing there is another significant step forward for our sport,” he said.

“The fact that an iconic capital like Madrid wants to join the calendar shows the strength of our sport and the momentum we continue to build around the world.”

title: Charles Leclerc 'flaw' pinned after latest Monza crash disaster
excerpt:
Former Formula 1 driver David Coulthard has identified Charles Leclerc's key "flaw" as being that the Ferrari driver has "whiteouts", following his huge accident in the Italian Grand Prix.

For the second time in his F1 career, Leclerc crashed out at Parabolica, silencing the Tifosi at the end of what was only the second lap.

Leclerc ran wide at the final turn while defending against Oscar Piastri, before dipping two tyres beyond the white line on the outside of the corner and touching a lengthy drain cover.

It unsettled the Monegasque's SF-26 and appeared to catch Leclerc by surprise, as his car darted off into the barrier at high speed.

He suffered temporary vision problems after the accident, but was quickly cleared by the medical centre as being okay.

It was a similar accident to the one that saw Leclerc crash out of the 2020 Italian GP, with him proving to have a tendency to make mistakes in costly situations.

Coulthard is unsure exactly how Leclerc has managed to crash twice at a turn where very few incidents occur, but has described the Ferrari driver as being prone to an occasional "glitch".

Discussing Leclerc's crash, Coulthard told the Up to Speed podcast: "Charles Leclerc is really, really talented because he's managed to crash in the same place twice, and I'm trying to get my head round a corner where you don't normally crash, especially there.

"What is it with him that's enabled him to get it wrong at the same place and have kind of the same crash twice? And I can only imagine the flaw in his brilliance is he has kind of whiteouts.

"He just has a little glitch, and at that moment of the glitch, it's so difficult to put into words, he just gets it wrong, doesn't he?

"Which, thankfully, he was okay. But huge crash, and done that in '20 and '26? It's pretty impressive."

title: F1 teams facing significant unknown as Madring makes debut
excerpt:
F1 is gearing up for a special weekend in Madrid. The new Madrid circuit, where the Spanish Grand Prix will be held for the first time this weekend, immediately poses a serious challenge for the teams.

According to initial analyses, the combination of fast straights and technical turns makes it difficult to identify a clear favourite in advance.

The new circuit bears some resemblance to well-known F1 tracks in several respects.

The fast section is reminiscent of Jeddah, while the more technical part shows similarities to Miami. It is precisely this combination that makes it interesting to see which car will adapt best.

For the teams, it will mainly be a matter of finding the right setup. The cars must perform well both in the fast sections and in the slower turns, and a choice that yields an advantage in one section may actually cost time elsewhere.

Another major unknown is the asphalt. Since the entire circuit is new, grip is likely to change significantly over the course of the weekend. As more cars drive on the track, the asphalt will become increasingly worn in. This can have major consequences for performance and tyre wear.

The fast corners, in particular, can put a heavy strain on the tyres. The most notable of these is 'La Monumental', a long turn with a banking angle of no less than 24 degrees.

Combined with the rapid succession of direction changes, this can cause the tyres to slide significantly across the asphalt.

This means that the teams must not only focus on the speed of their cars but also on how well they can preserve the tyres. On a new track, this can also change constantly throughout the weekend.

Who is the favourite?

On paper, Mercedes should once again be among the contenders, but the characteristics of the W17 mean that the Madrid circuit isn’t automatically an ideal track for the team.

The Mercedes is expected to be strong in the fast sections. In the technical sectors, however, the car may struggle more. The behaviour of the rear of the car, in particular, could play a role there, as Mercedes does not currently appear to be prioritising maximum rear stability.

Ferrari, on the other hand, could benefit from the track’s layout. With its characteristics, the SF-26 seems well-suited for the compromise required in Madrid. This gives Ferrari a chance to bounce back from its disappointing weekend at Monza.

The engine’s performance will also be interesting to watch. At Monza, Ferrari already demonstrated strong top speed on the long straight, but the car couldn’t maintain that advantage everywhere.

The fast section of the Madrid circuit could therefore serve as an interesting barometer for the power and efficiency of the powertrain.

McLaren also deserves special mention. The MCL40 has a relatively short wheelbase and isn’t known for having the lowest aerodynamic drag. Yet it is precisely this combination of characteristics that could work well on the Madring.

The car is known for its good handling and precision when entering corners. That could be a significant advantage, especially in the technical section.

If McLaren manages to maintain sufficient speed there without losing too much time on the straights, the team could be a serious contender for the win.

And then there’s Red Bull. The circuit features relatively few of the long, fast corners where the RB22 has sometimes struggled this season. La Monumental is a notable exception.

In the rest of the circuit, Red Bull’s strengths should shine through more clearly. The engine should also be well-suited to the track’s characteristics in the fast sections.

Furthermore, energy consumption in Madrid appears likely to be less of an issue than it was during the Italian Grand Prix.

All things considered, it is therefore particularly difficult to single out one clear favorite in advance. Mercedes, Ferrari, McLaren, and Red Bull all seem to have qualities that could allow them to perform strongly at the Madrid circuit.

As a result, the new track could very well lead to a surprising balance of power. In particular, the development of the track surface, tyre wear, and car setup will be decisive factors.

title: George Russell handed F1 title chances hammer blow
excerpt:
A RacingNews365 poll has delivered a damning verdict on George Russell's championship aspirations, with 74.9 per cent of voters declaring his title fight is over following the Italian Grand Prix.

Only 25.1 per cent of respondents believe Russell can still mount a comeback, a figure that looks increasingly optimistic given the scale of the task ahead.

Russell crossed the line second at Monza, less than four seconds behind team-mate Kimi Antonelli, but the result only deepened his problems.

Antonelli charged from 19th on the grid to claim a stunning victory, extending his championship lead to 66 points with likely nine races remaining.

Russell led for large portions of the afternoon, only for a Virtual Safety Car period to allow Mercedes to split strategies. Antonelli pitted for fresh rubber while Russell stayed out, a decision that proved decisive when the Italian carved past him three laps from the chequered flag.

Russell himself appeared to accept the reality of the situation in his post-race comments. "Definitely Kimi's in control of it and he's deserving to be in control of it," he told reporters at Monza.

"For me personally, I'm not even thinking about a fight or a comeback or anything. I'm just focused on taking it race by race and trying to maximise every single weekend."

With well over 200 points still available, the maths technically remain in Russell's favour, but that requires near-perfection from here and a significant collapse from Antonelli.

Factor in a looming engine penalty, with Mercedes confirming Russell has exhausted his allocation of penalty-free power units, and the road back looks steeper still.

Our readers, it seems, have already made up their minds.

title: Max Verstappen defends talks with rival F1 teams: 'Nothing wrong with that'
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has insisted there was “nothing wrong” with exploring other F1 options before committing to Red Bull.

Earlier this year, the four-time champion's future was in the air amid Red Bull's slip in the pecking order.

After being linked to Mercedes during 2025, this year saw his name associated with a move to McLaren before he penned an extension with Red Bull until at least the end of 2030.

It put an end to any speculation that Verstappen may opt to jump ship in the near future.

But when asked how serious his conversations were with rival teams, Verstappen told BBC Sport: "Of course, any kind of chat you take seriously.

“They're all very respectful chats. There's nothing wrong with that.

"I felt that staying was, for me, the right choice. You have to follow your heart.

“I could have run away very early on in my Red Bull career and gone somewhere else to try and win.

“If you have a little bit of patience, you do end up winning. I feel like that's my approach now as well."

Red Bull has endured a challenging start to the sport's new era under fresh technical regulations.

After 13 rounds, it is yet to take to the top step of the podium, with Verstappen enduring his longest victory drought in eight years.

Nevertheless, the Dutchman insisted he still felt Red Bull was the right option for his future.

"It comes down to also feeling well within a team,” he explained. “This is like a second family to me.

"The belief that you can turn things around, you can build towards hopefully a better future with other people, new people.

“And at the end of the day, it's not only Formula 1 for me. There are a lot of things that I'm doing next year that Red Bull is involved in as well.

"I feel good here. So this, for me, is the right place to be."

title: Audi point to Red Bull influence behind stunning F1 turnaround
excerpt:
Audi boss Allan McNish has pointed to the influence of former Red Bull chief mechanic Lee Stevenson for the team's turnaround in trackside operations, including pit-stops.

Stevenson, who rose through the Red Bull ranks to become chief mechanic to Max Verstappen, left in 2024 to join Sauber/Stake as it prepared for Audi's 2026 arrival.

Stevenson has now been promoted into the team manager role at Audi, a role similar to that which Jonathan Wheatley held at Red Bull, during which time his pit-crew was regarded as the best in the pit-lane, holding the world record for the fastest pit-stop until McLaren pinched it at the 2023 Qatar GP with a 1.8s stop for Lando Norris.

At the Dutch and Italian Grands Prix, Audi set the fastest pit-stop during the races, a remarkable rise from 2024 when the team was battling a costly technical issue in its stops, involving the wheel nuts.

Reflecting on the efforts at Zandvoort and Monza, racing director McNish pointed to Stevenson's influence on the team's trackside operations.

"It was a technical issue; it was in 2024, actually, and it was the technical issue at that point," McNish told media, including RacingNews365, when first presented with a question about the pit-stops.

"And this has been an area that's been worked on really through the end of last year, beginning of this year. In terms of the team, so Lee, who came to us last year, middle of 2025, he's got a good feel for what we needed to do.

"At the end of the day, the team there is the same people pretty much, and they're delivering it very, very well and consistently now. Because in Zandvoort, it was always the quickest as well, and also the other thing from my point of view, it's not just necessarily one stop, but when we have multiple stops, all the stops are good, and so the team there are working very well.

"That's important for us as well because we've got to take every advantage out of the race that we can. It's not as if there's much of a delta in this midfield, and so they've definitely delivered the opportunity for the drivers to take more out of the race.

"I wouldn't say we inherited [Stevenson's strengths], but I think we we have developed it. But at the end of the day, that was one of the reasons that Lee came on board was to build the team within the garage.

"I think he and the team that's in there have done a very good job. You just see them now, the way that they conduct not just the pit stops but also all of the work on the cars. It's very good to see."
